query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy, brittle behavior emerges at intermediate service temperatures because fast, temperature-driven nanosegregation of the alloy’s principal elements (e.g., Ni, Cr, and Mn) accumulates at grain boundaries, reducing local cohesion and promoting intergranular cracking under load. Engineering the alloy to include controlled, preexisting Cr-rich grain boundary precipitates can absorb the embrittling segregants and thereby mitigate GB decohesion and brittleness.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi or a similar system) in its as-cast or homogenized condition with no preexisting secondary phases at the grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled heat-treatment step (or alloying modification) that induces the formation of Cr-rich precipitates selectively at the grain boundaries, thereby creating a dual-phase microstructure where the precipitates are strategically distributed along the GBs.
generation.conditions: The alloy is evaluated under service-relevant conditions such as intermediate to high testing temperatures (e.g., around 650–700°C) and under tensile or creep loading regimes that mimic demanding engineering service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary regions, where the presence of Cr-rich precipitates acts as sinks for the mobile, embrittling principal elements.
generation.mechanism: At service temperatures, in the absence of preexisting precipitates, fast nanosegregation of elements like Ni, Cr, and Mn to grain boundaries reduces GB cohesion, leading to brittle intergranular fracture. With preexisting Cr-rich precipitates present, these phases preferentially absorb the segregants, reducing their concentration at the active GB and retaining ductile behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline single-phase alloy, the engineered dual-phase alloy with grain boundary Cr-rich precipitates will exhibit higher fracture strains and more ductile fracture features (e.g., dimpled rupture) during intermediate temperature tensile or creep tests, whereas the unmodified alloy will show intergranular brittle cracks.
generation.baseline: The single-phase high-entropy alloy in its homogenized state without any intentional grain boundary precipitates.
generation.boundary: Service conditions at intermediate temperatures (e.g., approximately 650–700°C) under tensile or creep loading, where conventional alloys typically show GB embrittlement due to segregation.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies support GB segregation leading to embrittlement in similar alloys, the precise quantitative improvement in ductility resulting from the introduced precipitates remains uncertain until experimentally measured.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens from the same base composition: one set remains as a homogenized single-phase alloy (control), and the other undergoes a tailored heat treatment to induce Cr-rich precipitates at the grain boundaries (intervention). Subject both sets to tensile and/or creep tests at the targeted intermediate temperatures (e.g., 650–700°C).
measurements: Fracture surface analysis (e.g., SEM) to determine intergranular versus transgranular fracture modes
Measurement of ductility (fracture strain) and tensile properties
Characterization of grain boundary chemistry via techniques such as APT or STEM-EDS to confirm segregation patterns
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the intervention (grain boundary precipitate engineering) does not result in a statistically significant improvement in ductility or if both the treated and untreated alloys display similar intergranular brittle failure and comparable GB segregation profiles, then the hypothesis that preexisting precipitates mitigate embrittlement by trapping segregating elements would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The ductility loss in metals and alloys can be related to the segregation of impurity elements at GBs (, ) and the absorption of hydrogen or helium (), which weaken GB strength and promote crack initiation at GBs, and the precipitation of second phases (intermetallic compounds, carbides, nitrides, oxides, etc.) at GBs (, ), which causes high stress/strain concentration due to the incompatibility of elastic and plastic deformation between particles and matrix. In contrast to carbides and nitrides, intermetallic compound–induced embrittlement at room temperature can be relieved at high temperatures because plastic codeformation between these compounds and the matrix can reduce stress concentration and, thus, delay crack initiation (). cited_evidence.text: Segregation of minor alloying elements to GBs often embrittles conventional alloys (, ). Grain refinement is an effective way to evade GB embrittlement because more interfaces reduce the level of individual GB segregation (). In contrast, multiple principal constitutive elements in HEAs can segregate into GBs instead of trace alloying elements. In HEAs, grain refinement can assist the segregation of principal constitutive elements to GBs and even lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases at GBs (). For example, Cr-rich bcc phases and L10-NiMn phases precipitate at GBs in nanocrystalline Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (grain size, ~50 nm) after annealing at 450°C for only 5 min, which reduces the ductility substantially (). In addition, previous studies show that Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEAs with the grain sizes from 4.4 to 155 μm all exhibit loss of ductility at intermediate temperatures, irrespective of grain size in this range (Fig. 1). Microalloying with B in Fe-Mn steels has been reported to delay temper embrittlement at 450°C (). B can compete for GB sites and reduce GB energy and, thus, repel the embrittling element Mn due to the decreased driving force for Mn segregation
